answers.stem_only: Spread the instances across at least two Availability Zones (for example an Auto Scaling group over subnets in several zones) and register them all with the existing Application Load Balancer so it routes around a failed zone.

Because an outage on zone failure is acceptable and traffic is small, use a single NAT gateway in one public subnet and point all private route tables' default routes to it; per-zone NAT gateways cost more for availability that is not required.

Use IAM Identity Center connected to the existing external identity provider, define permission sets, and assign users or groups to the accounts they need; access uses short-term credentials and is managed centrally.
Add a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3 and route the private subnets' S3 prefix list to it; it is private, has no hourly or data processing charge, and removes the NAT gateway from the path.
Use managed NAT gateways, one in a public subnet in each Availability Zone, with each private subnet routed to the NAT gateway in its own zone; no patching and zone-independent.

One NAT gateway in a public subnet in each of the three Availability Zones, each private route table pointing to the NAT gateway in its own zone; this is the cheapest design that survives a zone failure.

Create one IAM role with a policy scoped to read objects in that single bucket and a trust policy for Amazon EC2, attach it to the instances through an instance profile, and remove the stored access key.

Because on-premises servers over Direct Connect must also reach S3 privately and gateway endpoints cannot be used from on premises, create an interface VPC endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) for Amazon S3 in the VPC, used by both the instances and the data center.
Use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager with no inbound ports open, and enable session logging to Amazon S3 or CloudWatch Logs for audit.

Block the range with an inbound deny rule in the network ACL of the load balancer's subnets (security groups cannot deny), numbered before the allow rules; and set the instance security group to allow HTTPS only from the load balancer's security group.
Create a service control policy that denies ec2:DeleteFlowLogs and attach it once at the organization root so it applies to all member accounts, including their root users.

Run the instances in an Auto Scaling group across private subnets in two Availability Zones behind the load balancer, and add a NAT gateway in the second zone with each private subnet routed to the NAT gateway in its own zone; no multi-Region setup.
